posts.content_md:
Hi!

I would like to ask a stupid question about silver halide film.

BB640 plates are developed in a developer and bleached in

a second bath that dissolves the silver aggregates that are

formed in the emulsion during developing. 

According to my book about holography and other information

this should be correct. 

So there is no step that removes all silver halide

from the emulsion like it is done in a fixing bath in usual

photography.

But my BB640 plates turn dark within a very short period

because light decomposes the silver halide in the emulsion.

I wonder if this is acceptable and how this can be prevented. 

Doesn't the dark silver absorb too much light?

posts.content_md:
> **Fred:** Hi!I would like to ask a stupid question about silver halide film.BB640 plates are developed in a developer and bleached ina second bath that dissolves the silver aggregates that areformed in the emulsion during developing.According to my book about holography and other informationthis should be correct.So there is no step that removes all silver halidefrom the emulsion like it is done in a fixing bath in usualphotography.

Speaking of reflection holograms: unless you apply special techniques like SHSG, some colloidal developers etc., no fixing is involved.

The following section is taken from Richard Birenheide's 1997 website. Birenheide had designed the HRT emulsion - the processing baths baths were based on Jeff Blyth's ascorbic acid developer (now called "JD-4") and his copper sulfate bleach.

"Suggested Processing Formulae

Rehalogenating process

a. Developer

700 cc water (deionized, if available)

70 g sodium carbonate, anhydrous

15 g sodium hydroxide*

4 g metol (4-(methylamino)-phenol-sulfate)

25 g ascorbic acid

add water to 1000 cc

Please allow any constituent to dissolve be-

fore adding the next on the list. It is important 

to limit the time the surface of this developer 

is exposed to air (oxygen). Therefore the use 

of two closely fitting plastic dishes is strongly 

recommended so that one dish floats 

("floating lid") on top of the developer and 

the only time the whole surface is exposed to 

air is when the development progress is being 

monitored. Develop to a density of at least 

2.5. Minimum development time: 3 min.

b. Stop bath

1000 cc water (deionized, if available)

5 g sodium hydrogen sulfate* crystals

Rinse briefly in cold water and then bleach.

c. Bleach

700 cc water (deionized, if available)

35 g copper sulfate (pentahydrate)*

100 g potassium bromide

5 g sodium hydrogen sulfate crystals*

add water to 1000 cc

Bleach until the hologram is clear. Rinse in 

cold water for at least 5 min. Normally, unless you

are making reflection master holograms, this bleach 

should always be followed by an "anti-print 

out" bath such as:-

d. Anti printout

700 cc water (deionized, if available)

3 g potassium dichromate

6 g sodium hydrogen sulfate

add water to 1000 cc

Treat for about 1 minute with agitation.

To rinse off, just give a brief dip in a bath of 

deionized water free of any trace of devel-

oper. The brevity of the rinse is necessary to 

actually leave some of the anti-printout solu-

tion within the body of the hologram. 

Please note that dichromate is a toxic material 

and treated unprotected holograms should 

not be handled by young children.

This "anti-print out" has the additional advan-

tage that it will break down any residual dye 

present in the emulsion from sensitization. 

However, with the "pyrochrome" system (see 

below) that bleach will serve as a dye 

remover."

> But my BB640 plates turn dark within a very short periodbecause light decomposes the silver halide in the emulsion.I wonder if this is acceptable and how this can be prevented.Doesn't the dark silver absorb too much light?]

At what moment do they turn dark?

posts.content_md:
Hi!

> **Martin:** Speaking of reflection holograms: unless you apply special techniques like SHSG, some colloidal developers etc., no fixing is involved.

Yes, I was very surprised first that holograms are usually not fixed

but I suppose fixing would probably reduce the variations of the index of

refraction and ruin a hologram.

> The following section is taken from Richard Birenheide's 1997 website. Birenheide had designed the HRT emulsion - the processing baths baths were based on Jeff Blyth's ascorbic acid developer (now called "JD-4") and his copper sulfate bleach.

I still have a copy of this page and I used these suggestions.

They are fortunately also in the Internet Archive here:

[http://web.archive.org/web/200102010649 ... t-gmbh.de/](http://web.archive.org/web/20010201064900/http://www.hrt-gmbh.de/)

Perhaps I will try out the other process you mentioned because

I wasn't happy with the diffraction efficiency in the other process.

> d. Anti printout700 cc water (deionized, if available)3 g potassium dichromate6 g sodium hydrogen sulfateadd water to 1000 cc

I used the pyrochrome process so I omitted the anti printout

bath because the finished holograms looked yellow because 

of dichromate in the emulsion.

> At what moment do they turn dark?

They turn dark after a few hours of sunlight or a longer period

in a room with fluorescent lamps. This is no surprise because the

silver halide is still in the emulsion and can be decomposed by

the light. 

Is it a general disadvantage of silver halide films for holography

and is it avoided by storing the holograms in the dark?

[quote:385a8080ef="Fred"]Hi!

I would like to ask a stupid question about silver halide film.

BB640 plates are developed in a developer and bleached in

a second bath that dissolves the silver aggregates that are

formed in the emulsion during developing. 

According to my book about holography and other information

this should be correct. 

So there is no step that removes all silver halide

from the emulsion like it is done in a fixing bath in usual

photography.

But my BB640 plates turn dark within a very short period

because light decomposes the silver halide in the emulsion.

I wonder if this is acceptable and how this can be prevented. 

Doesn't the dark silver absorb too much light?[/quote:385a8080ef]

It depends on the bleach. A reversal bleach will remove the silver and leave just the silver halide, a rehalogenating bleach will rehalogenate the reduced silver. This sounds crazy since you've just put back the silver halide you've reduced. We talked on this in the old forum, but I can't find the thread.

The periodic structure of the fringes causes diffraction, but also there is absorption of the black silver and scattering from both reduced silver and halide. Whic process dominates depends on the grain density inside the emulsion and the fringe structure. If the fringes are sinusoidal diffraction is very strong.

In any cae, you need to wash thoroughly both in between develop and bleach and after bleach. 

I've written a small article on SilverHalide. It's not particularly deep (or even particularly good!) but it may give you an idea of the process:

[http://www.triple-take.com/Articles](http://www.triple-take.com/Articles)

Apparently my problem is called "print-out" or "printout" in

holography. There are some suggestions to avoid it but I

fear they are not very effective. I will look for further suggestions

in the patent literature and on the internet to avoid this problem.

I just found this patent about a bleach based on N-Bromsuccinimid (NBS):

 4,032,348 that should reduce print-out.

[http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Pars ... D+hologram](http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=/netahtml/search-bool.html&r=12&f=G&l=50&co1=AND&d=ptxt&s1=print-out&s2=hologram&OS=print-out+AND+hologram&RS=print-out+AND+hologram)

US Pat. 4,187,106

[http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Pars ... D+hologram](http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&p=1&u=/netahtml/search-bool.html&r=15&f=G&l=50&co1=AND&d=ptxt&s1=print-out&s2=hologram&OS=print-out+AND+hologram&RS=print-out+AND+hologram)

black/white transparencies (e.g. published by AGFA) and produces

There is also a new patent invented by SAMSUNG for SHSG from BB640

posts.content_md:
> **Fred:** Is it a general disadvantage of silver halide films for holography and is it avoided by storing the holograms in the dark?

The issue of permanence of holograms undoubtedly is a very controversial issue and has previously raised some discussions on network54, eg. [http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewt ... 86&start=0](http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=2286&start=0)

Storing the hologram in the dark would certainly prevent darkeningng to a large extent - that has been the approach to some early photographs...

> I just found this patent about a bleach based on N-Bromsuccinimid (NBS):4,032,348 that should reduce print-out.

Not sure if this really improves things.

> US Pat. 4,720,441 (...) suggests a KI bath and a further bleach bath forthe same purpose:

That's one of the classic methods. The downside is, it seems to increase grain size (causing severe scatter on emulsions having larger grains).

> US Pat. 4,187,106 (...) is perhaps the best solution because it removes all silver salts from the emulsion. It looks like the common process for the production ofblack/white transparencies (e.g. published by AGFA) and producesa kind of SHSG.

Agreed. That method by Gladden will be limited to low spatial frequencies though.

> There is also a new patent invented by SAMSUNG for SHSG from BB640plates: (...) I wonder if somebody already used those methods.

On network54 we extensively discussed the forerunner(s) of that patent. I have never tried that method with BB emulsions but believe that, due to their initial hardness, that process is likely to require some fine tuning.

I also found it odd that your printout was so quick. I have BB640, BB520 and BB450 that's from a year old to a few months old with no, or very slight, printout. These are both reflection and transmission. Usually printout occurs because you're not washing well enough between developing and bleaching, or you're not fixing. Perhaps try a stop bath between development and bleach. 

One quick thought occurs to me. Are they in a high UV environment?

> IntroductionThese are preliminary instructions for the use of BB-plates together with some of their characteristics. These plates are designed for ease of use in common with conventional Western type silver halide material. The plates have been tested with the common types of developer and bleach such as the "pyrochrome system" or alternatively a developer based on ascorbic acid and either a ferric EDTA bleach or a bleach based on copper sulfate (Blyth's recipe; see below). However, you can try your favorite system possibly allowing longer development times than you are used to.Plate characteristicsThese plates are mainly intended for the use in display holography. Therefore we try to produce the finest grain size of silver halide and at the same time a good light sensitivity. (Light sensitivity is unfortunately inversely related to grain size). The smaller the grain size the less the scatter or milkiness in a correctly exposed and processed hologram.We have found that our product has noticeably less scatter than that of a well known competitive product but the exposure time does need to be at least three times that of the well known product. This emulsion is hardened quite strongly. If you would like to make reflection holograms with a more broadband replay please ask for plates which are less hardened.Storage conditions for plates should be cool, around 4 C but not below 0 C!Please allow the plates to equilibrate with the relative humidity and temperature of your lab once you have opened the polyethylene bag before shooting holograms. For making masters (H 1) this is of paramount importance. For these, intensity distribution of the reference beam should be as uniform as possible.A very useful tip comes from Inaki Beguiristain from Spatial Imaging, England: to find out the emulsion side of a plate, breathe carefully on the suspected side: the emulsion side does not become frosty because the gelatin absorbs the moisture. Please allow extra settling time after doing this in order to remove the water before exposure.If exposure time is too long compared to what you are used to with conventional material, please try to use a higher reference/object beam ratio in multiple beam setups. It's fairly dangerous and I wouldn't recommend anyone to use it, but

PBQ:

p-Benzoquinone..............2g

Citric Acid.................15g

Potassium Bromide...........50g

I would use PBU-amidol with CWC2:

Potassium Persulphate.......10g

Citric Acid.................50g

Cupric Bromide..............1g

Potassium Bromide...........10g

> Is PBQ a bleach using p-Benzoquinone?

The very best PBU formula in my view is PBU-metol:

cupric bromide....................1g

potassium persulphate.......10g 

citric acid...........................50g 

potassium bromide............20g 

metol...................................1g

> **Martin:** Yes, as Dinesh pointed out, it's considered quite toxic. I understand the health risk mainly stems from handling PBQ as a solid, in „dust“ form (a problem it may share with stuff like dichromates).

To me this remark was rather surprising because both 

the p-benzoquinone and hydroquinone form a redox pair 

(you perhaps know the "Chinhydron"-electrode)

and therefore I wouln't expect a big difference in toxicological data.

I just looked the toxicity of p-Benzoquinone up and it is apparently

classified as toxic (T-label) since over 20 years (at least in Europe).

But p-Benzoquinone and Hydroquinone are both mutagenic to some 

extent.

I suppose the different classification as T (for Benzoquinone)

and Xn (for Hydrochinon) is based on acute toxicology data. 

Benzoquinone has apparently a LD50 of 130 mg/kg while for Hydrochinon 

320 mg/kg are cited. The legal upper limit for a classification as T is an 

LD50 (oral, rat) of 200 mg/kg.

This is the reason why one chemical is T while the other is only Xn.

(It is probably similar to the situation for some Barium salts although 

Barium is the toxic ion. Barium chloride is toxic now, too because of an 

LD50 of about 180 mg/kg while other soluble Barium salts with heavier 

anions like the acetate, chlorate or iodide (or even the chloride as a 

dihydrate) have an LD50 of perhaps 220-230 mg/kg and are not toxic 

according to the EU-regulation 67/548/EWG.)

So this is more or less a legal question. From a toxicological point

of view p-benzoquinone is only a factor 2.5 more toxic than hydroquinone. 

For the dichromates the situation is even more crazy. It is known

that CrO3 and chromates/dichromates are carcinogenic since the 1930s.

But before the new version of the German regulation about

dangerous chemicals was introduced in 1994 they were classified only

as "irritant" (Xi) from the legal point of view. Since about 10 years they 

are "very toxic" if inhaled (T+), "toxic" if ingested because all class

2 and class 1 carcinogens are automatically "toxic" by law.

On the other hand it is known that many chemicals and even oak wood 

dust are carcinogens when inhaled. So more and more rather harmless 

chemicals (like cobalt chloride, blue silica gel) and oak/beech wood dust 

were classified as "toxic" recently -with all legal consequences. 

In my opinion this is not a good idea because it is already known

that much more solid substances might act as carcinogens if inhaled. 

To me dichromates were toxic to some extent before 1994 and

I don't panic when I see blue silica gel although our university

instructed all employees to use gloves and even gas masks when 

removing blue gel when the legal classification was changed four years 

ago.

> However there is another PBU bleach formula that allows in situ PBQ formation (it takes about 2 hours to form the PBQ):cupric bromide....................1gpotassium persulphate.......10gcitric acid...........................50gpotassium bromide............20ghydroquinone (quinol).........1gwater...................................1 L

Thank you for the hint. This version would form the p-benzoquinone in the 

solution and this would make e.g. things easier for private purchasers that 

are now hindered by a new ban of mail order sales of toxic chemicals 

to purchase the quinone.

posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** Can you explain LD50 for us? I know a little about it but I am not sure everyone here does and I think it is very important.

The LD50 is the lethal dose, that causes deaths of 50% of animals in

an experiment. The European Union defines a LD50 of 200 mg/kg

for oral ingestion for rats as the limit to classify chemicals as toxic.

Chemicals with 200mg/kg-2000 mg/kg are classified as harmful (Xn).

You can compare those values with those of common chemicals

as ethanol (LD50 about 7000 mg/kg), sodium carbonate

(about 4000 mg/kg) or Barium nitrate (355 mg/kg), silver nitrate

(1173 mg/kg). Rather toxic chemicals like HgCl2 have an LD50 of

1 mg/kg, KCN has 5 mg/kg.

For Hydroquinone a value of 320 mg/kg was given. So 640 mg 

Hydroquinone could kill a rat with a weight of 2 kg. 

For p-Benzoquinone a smaller dose would produce a similar result.

> **Martin:** [Interesting! So if I understand you correctly, the LD does say absolutely nothing about health risks involving long-term exposure to a particular chemical agent?

Yes, the LD50 concept for acute toxicology as the base to classify the dangers of chemicals has many shortcomings. 

It isn't possible to predict the dangers long-term effects of small doses from 

an LD50 value. This is usually described as chronic toxicology.

Therefore the rule that all class 1+2 carcinogenic or mutagenic substances are classified as toxic chemicals, too, was added.

> **Dinesh:** Thank you for an explanation of toxicity. While I did know about LD50, I did not know the actual numbers that classified materials.

Perhaps I should add a few remarks about toxicology and safety.

For example sodium nitrite has an LD50 of 180 mg/kg and is therefore officially toxic. On the other hand it is not very dangerous to use it and even if a small amount is spilled it is only removed later. 

It is even used in small amounts in food (for mixtures and solutions the toxicity is calculated: e.g. a 0.5% KCN solution is only harmful according to the law). 

For chemicals that are more dangerous or that should be kept away

from the skin (e.g. if they are resorbed through the skin) I would wear gloves. Once I had an accident with a large bottle of Sodium fluoride (LD50 52 mg/kg) when I tried to open the old plastic bottle. I usually wouldn't

have used gloves but I was happy that I used them when the whole

bottle broke apart and the result was a large pile of about 1 kg sodium fluoride in the hood and a large amount on the gloves... 

For very toxic chemicals (with an LD50<25 mg/kg like As2O3 etc.) 

more care is required and gloves are worn and any spilling is usually avoided.

> What I'm curious about in p-Benzoquinone is that it's properties as a dust is what causes it to be classified as a toxin. Apparently it's dust is carcinogenic at a few mg.

For Dichromates the carcinogenic dust was one of the reasons why they are toxic chemicals in Europe now. In my opinion the classification of p-Benzoquinone is based on the LD50 value (acute toxicology)

but I will look the details at least for Europe up. 

According to the European classification it is toxic by ingestion

and inhalation and irritating (skin, eyes).

Apparently EPA doesn't classify it as a carcinogen:

[http://www.epa.gov/ttn/atw/hlthef/quinone.html](http://www.epa.gov/ttn/atw/hlthef/quinone.html)

> However, LD50 seems to require ingestion.

There are also values of inhalation of toxic chemicals (e.g. chlorine gas).

> So would an LD50 figure correlate with toxicity in the case of a carcinogenic dust.

No, a LD50 figure has nothing to do with carcinogenic properties.

But all class 1+2 carcinogenic chemicals are classified as toxic 

here in Europe. The lower legal limit for compositions is usually 

a concentration of less than 0.01% but this is of course only a 

legal definition.

> Also, since the stuff is a carcinogen, how could one correlate cancer with oral ingestion over long term?

According to the above EPA homepage they don't consider

p-Benzoquinone to be a carcinogen but there are at least

some hints in the literature that hydroquinone and p-benzoquinone

might have some mutagenic properties. 

> The situation over here is crazy as well. Especially over this "Chromium 6" scare as a result of the movie about the lawyer a few years back. The funny thing is that a OSCHA employee (Occupation Safety and Health-something. The body that administers and enforces such things as storage and disposal of chemicals in the workplace) actually saw a 500gm bottle of Potassium Dichromate and didn't realise he was looking at "Chromium 6"! The rules surrounding the disposal of minute amounts of chemical developers, fixers and bleaches are so meaningless (and expsensive) in the quantities that most holographers use them that most of us admit to flushing them.

In my opinion this panic is ridiculous. But here in Germany some bureaucrats nearly panicked when they once only saw such a bottle in a company according to a story the owner told me. The local health authority

had to calm them down . In German schools the funny vulcano

experiment was even banned only because of fears a chromium-chromate

on the EU list of possible carcinogens might form in this experiment

although there is no hint in the literature that this might be true.

It is quite easy to dispose dichromates. You can reduce them to Cr(III) e.g. with sodium sulfite and Cr(III) compounds are no longer toxic. 

(Cr2O3 is for example not even a hazmat chemical according to the German regulations). 

In Germany things are easier because cost-free disposal is usually 

offered for private users and small amounts from small companies.

> We have to store our bleach in a large bucket and dispose of it through a chemical disposal company when the bucket is full. Since we make maybe 3 to 6 silver holograms in a month, the stuff evaporates faster than we can fill it. But we still must show evidence of storing these minute quatities in this giant bucket.

I can imagine it. In Germany things are similar for companies that

use such chemicals.

> A friend of mine who's a chemist recently told me that he spilled a small drop of Mercury. He was quite willing to simply scoop it off the floor. But he was required to call OSCHA who came in full CNB suits, isolated the plant, declared an emergency and then surrounded the offensive drop with vaccuums. Crazy!

I can imagine it because here frequently similar incidents occur.

It would be common practice to dispose the mercury e.g. with

Zinc powder (there is for example a Merck kit for this purpose)

but the whole street can be evecuated because of such a small

accident if the fire brigade is called...

The new Cobalt-panic here in Europe is even funnier. 

Some bureaucrats forget the old wisdom even Paracelsus (1493-1541)

knew that there are no inherently dangerous and harmless chemicals 

and that the dose and use determines the danger.

All cobalt compounds and even blue silica gel with only 0.01-0.1% Co 

are now classified as "toxic" although cobalt is even an 

essential element for the body.

On the other hand some vitamine pills contain e.g. Vitamine B12 that

contains cobalt or even considerable amounts of cobalt chloride...

I saw that in Canada there was some trouble because of asbest

traces in Vermiculite while some bureaucrats make trouble because of

small asbest traces in talkum. In my opinion this is ridiculous

because the "danger" of such talkum powder with less than

0.01% asbest is only a legal problem. Experts estimated that even

during 30 years (8 hours per day) in a thick dust cloud there would

be no risk...
